One hour before

Monday 3 May 2038, ten in the morning, in the garden in La Duchère park, one hour before the inauguration. The plaque is still covered with a white sheet. Rose-Hélène, ten, has in her pocket the letter Odile left her in 2031, “for later”.
Isabelle, I’ve been keeping this letter for seven years. I put it in my drawer seven years ago, and I’ve never opened it.
I know. Ever since you learnt to read, you’ve often looked at it, haven’t you?
Not often. Only when I need her. This morning, when I woke up, I knew it was time.
Do you want to open it now, before everyone arrives?
No. I’ll open it at the moment they take the sheet off the plaque. Not before.
My mother would have liked that. She used to say you only open a door when someone knocks.
While we wait for the mayor, we could rehearse the waltz one last time.
We’ve rehearsed it for three months, Dad. I’ve known it by heart since I was two.
Then let’s wait. As soon as the others are here, we’ll start.
Look, Viorica is getting off the bus. And Haruka’s grandmother is with her!
They speak neither the same language nor use the same alphabet, but they’re walking arm in arm.
Maybe that’s what my mother wanted to teach us. You don’t always need words to understand each other.
(she touches the letter in her pocket) One more hour. I’ve waited seven years, I can certainly wait one more.

1. Expressing time
French has different expressions for a past moment, for a duration that is still going on and for a duration that is over. Learners often mix them up:
il y a + duration
… ago (a past moment)
Je l’ai reçue il y a sept ans.
depuis + duration / ça fait… que
for… / since… (an ongoing duration, verb in the PRESENT)
Je la garde depuis sept ans. / Ça fait sept ans que je la garde.
pendant + duration
for… (a finished duration)
On l’a répétée pendant trois mois.
en + duration
in… (the time needed)
Il a lu le livre en une nuit.
dans + duration
in… (from now, in the future)
Dans une heure, on commence.
Trap: with “depuis”, French uses the PRESENT for an action that is still going on: “Je l’attends depuis une heure” (I’ve been waiting for her for an hour). “Je l’ai attendue depuis une heure” ✗.
quand / lorsque / dès que / au moment où
INDICATIVE (future for the future)
Dès que les autres seront là, on commencera.
depuis que / pendant que / après que
INDICATIVE
Depuis que tu sais lire…
avant que / jusqu’à ce que / en attendant que
En attendant que le maire arrive…
2. The pronouns y and en, double pronouns
Are you going to the garden? — Yes, I’m going there. (y = à + place)
Are you thinking about the letter? — I think about it every day. (y = à + thing)
Do you have memories of Odile? — I have lots. (en = de + …, quantity)
I’ve waited seven years, I can wait one more. (en + number)
The order of double pronouns before the verb:
Elle me la donne. Je le lui ai dit. Il y en a trois. In the affirmative imperative, the order changes: “Donne-la-moi !”, “Dis-le-lui !”.
For people, after “penser à” you don’t use “y” but “à lui / à elle”: “Je pense à Odile” → “Je pense à elle”, not “J’y pense” ✗.
3. Past participle agreement
The golden rule of B2:
Auxiliary
agrees with the subject
Elles sont arrivées hier.
no agreement with the subject
Elles ont chanté.
avoir + direct object BEFORE
agrees with the direct object
La lettre, je l’ai gardée. Les clés qu’elle a données.
avoir + en
no agreement
Des lettres, j’en ai reçu trois.

How to check: ask “what?” after the verb. If the answer (the direct object) is already written BEFORE the verb (a pronoun “la, les” or “que”), the participle agrees: “la valse qu’on a répétée” (répétée = la valse).
The typical mistake: “Les fleurs que j’ai acheté” ✗ → “Les fleurs que j’ai achetées” ✓. You can’t always hear the difference, but you can see it in the exam.
4. Emphasis: c’est… qui, c’est… que
To highlight one element of the sentence, you frame it with “c’est… qui” (for the subject) or “c’est… que” (for everything else):
Odile taught me to answer. → It was Odile who taught me to answer.
I’ll open it then. → It’s then that I’ll open it (and not at another time).
I’m the one who drew the cover.
After “c’est moi qui”, the verb agrees with “moi”: “C’est moi qui AI dessiné”, “C’est nous qui AVONS gagné”, not “c’est moi qui a” ✗.
5. Complex negations
Negation
ne… plus
no longer, not any more
Elle n’est plus là.
Je ne l’ai jamais ouverte.
only (a restriction, NOT a negation)
On n’ouvre une porte que quand quelqu’un frappe.
ne… guère
hardly (formal register)
Il ne parle guère.
ne… ni… ni
Elles ne parlent ni la même langue ni le même alphabet.
ne… personne / ne… rien
nobody / nothing
Je n’ai vu personne. Il n’a rien dit.
ne… plus personne / ne… jamais rien
combinations
Il n’y a plus personne. Elle ne demande jamais rien.
In the informal register, “ne” is dropped (“J’ai rien vu”), but in writing and in the exam you always keep it.

Plus tard

On Saturday 1 May 2038, Lyon woke up with lily of the valley on every street corner. It was the tradition: on that day, little bunches of white bell-shaped flowers, said to bring good luck, were sold on the pavements. At Part-Dieu station, Julien was waiting on platform four with three sprigs of lily of the valley in his hand, one for each of the travellers. Ioana was beside him. Henri-Ion, who was seven, was holding a sign he had made himself, with lots of glitter and a single spelling mistake: “Bienvenu Viorica”. Ioana had added an “e” in felt-tip, discreetly, on the metro.

Viorica had travelled for two nights and a day, from Bucharest to Vienna, from Vienna to Zurich, from Zurich to Lyon, with Ilinca carrying the suitcases and Professor Petrescu carrying the medicines, the sandwiches and the conversation. She was ninety-seven. The doctors in Bucharest had told her it was madness. She had replied that madness would be sitting in an armchair waiting for death when you could wait for it on a train, looking at the Alps. When she stepped off the carriage, very upright, with her stick and her grey hat, Henri-Ion held up his sign so high that he nearly fell over backwards.

On the platform, a little apart, there was also Simone Roux, ninety-two, with her stick and a bunch of lily of the valley much bigger than Julien’s. She had insisted on coming. She said an old lady arriving in a foreign city should be welcomed by another old lady, because young people don’t know what to say. The two women looked at each other for a long moment. Then Simone pointed at Viorica’s stick and said: “Mine is prettier.” Viorica replied: “Mine has seen more countries.” They burst out laughing at the same time, and Julien realised he would have nothing left to do all day.

Viorica was staying on rue d’Austerlitz, at Julien and Ioana’s, in Henri-Ion’s room; he had enthusiastically agreed to sleep in a tent in the living room for three nights. In the afternoon, Isabelle came to take her to see Odile’s flat, two floors up. Viorica climbed the stairs step by step, stopping on every landing to catch her breath and to say something unpleasant about architects who never thought about old people. In Odile’s living room there was the piano. Viorica sat down at it without asking. She played three notes, with one finger. Then she said: “It’s out of tune. Like me. That’s good.”

Isabelle gave her a copy of the book, the one she had set aside for her, with a dedication. Viorica had demanded an original, and now she had one. She read it that very evening, in Henri-Ion’s bed, under a dinosaur poster, until three in the morning. Ioana, who had got up for a glass of water, saw light under the door. She knocked softly. Viorica told her to come in. She had the book open at one of Odile’s pages, the one from 1992, about the young man from Kosovo and the word “tomorrow”. She said to Ioana: “You know, at my age, it’s the hardest word in any language. But I’m learning it all the same.”

On Saturday evening, Simone invited Viorica to dinner in Villeurbanne, in the flat in Gratte-Ciel. Farid had made a qabuli palaw for eight. Philippe had come from Paris especially, and for once the drawing of lots had spared him. After dinner, the two old ladies stayed alone on the balcony, with a blanket over their knees and a small glass of plum liqueur that Viorica had brought from Bucharest in her suitcase, wrapped in three jumpers. They talked until midnight. Viorica told the story of her father’s piano, pushed out of the window in 1950. Simone told the story of her father’s guitar, confiscated at the border in 1939. They fell silent for a moment. Then Viorica raised her glass: “To our fathers, who lost their instruments.” Simone added: “And to us, who kept on playing.”

On Sunday 2 May it was Haruka’s turn to wait. She had arrived at Saint-Exupéry airport two hours too early, with Isabelle, Farid and her violin, because she didn’t know what to do with her hands. She had put Odile’s pencil in her pocket, out of superstition. The plane from Helsinki was forty minutes late. Haruka paced up and down in front of the arrivals gate for forty minutes, so much so that Farid calculated she had walked at least three kilometres. Then the automatic doors opened, and she saw Aoi pushing a wheelchair. In the wheelchair, very small, in a navy-blue coat, was her grandmother.

Chiyo Mori was eighty-four. She had taught music for forty years in a primary school in Kyoto, and she had never left Japan. Haruka stopped three metres away from her. Following the rules she had been taught since childhood, she bowed deeply, hands on her knees. Her grandmother bowed too, as far as you can bow in a wheelchair. For two seconds they stayed like that, very proper, very Japanese. Then Chiyo opened her arms. And Haruka forgot all the rules she had been taught. She ran. Aoi had to hold the wheelchair so that it wouldn’t roll back from the impact.

In the taxi back to Lyon, Chiyo said almost nothing. She looked out of the window at the fields, the factories, the buildings, the Rhône, with the same attention she would have given to a concert. Haruka translated the road signs for her. Then, at the edge of the city, Chiyo took from her bag a little notebook in which she had written, in careful Latin letters, the only French sentence she had prepared during the journey, with Aoi’s help. She read it aloud, slowly, with an accent that turned every syllable into a musical note: “Hello, Lyon. I have come to answer.” The taxi driver, an old moustached Lyonnais, had to pull over onto the hard shoulder to blow his nose.

In the afternoon, Haruka took her grandmother to Gérard’s café. She wanted her to see the place where she had waited for her results, where she had drunk tea from Odile’s chipped cup, where the op-ed club had adopted her like a granddaughter. Gérard had been warned. He had put a white tablecloth on the best table, by the window. He served the tea in Odile’s cup, which Haruka had brought back for the occasion, and put a madeleine beside it on a little plate. Chiyo looked at the chipped cup for a long time. Then she said something in Japanese. Haruka translated: in Japan, broken cups are mended with gold, because a crack is part of an object’s story.

The op-ed club was there in full, of course, pretending to read the Sunday papers. Monsieur Castaing stood up, bowed to Chiyo with the stiffness of a Latin teacher, and recited a haiku by Bashō to her, in Japanese, which he had learnt by heart during the week by listening to a recording thirty times. His pronunciation was, according to Haruka, abominable. Chiyo listened to the end with the utmost seriousness, then applauded softly, three times. Monsieur Castaing went back to his seat, red as a tomato, and for the rest of the afternoon he didn’t correct anyone. Gérard said it was a miracle and should be reported to the Vatican.

In the evening there was a dinner at Julien and Ioana’s, on rue d’Austerlitz, with almost everyone. Tables had been set up right out onto the landing. For the first time, the two grandmothers who had come from afar met. Viorica didn’t speak Japanese. Chiyo spoke neither Romanian nor French, apart from her sentence in the taxi. They sat side by side, looked at each other, and began to talk, each in her own language, Viorica in French mixed with Romanian, Chiyo in Japanese, with lots of gestures. Haruka started to translate, then stopped. She realised they didn’t need it. They were talking about their fathers. You could see it in their hands.

Viorica’s father had been a pianist; his piano had been taken from him in 1950 and pushed out of the window. Chiyo’s father had played the koto, the great Japanese zither; during the war he had been forbidden to play, because traditional music was too “weak” for a country at war, and he had buried his instrument in the garden, wrapped in blankets. He dug it up in 1946. The wood had rotted. He never played again. When Haruka finally translated these two stories, from one language to the other, the whole table fell silent. Farid, at the end of the table, put his hand on his rubab case without saying anything.

Chiyo then took a small lacquered wooden box out of her bag. She opened it in front of everyone. Inside, on a piece of worn silk, there were three small picks of yellowed ivory, the kind you wear on your fingertips to pluck the strings of a koto. It was all that remained of her father’s instrument. The wood had rotted in the garden soil, but the picks, which he kept in his pocket, had survived the war. Chiyo took one and placed it in Viorica’s hand. Viorica looked at it for a long time. Then she rummaged in her handbag and took out a dried lime blossom, between two sheets of tissue paper, picked the previous summer from the 1946 lime tree outside the house in Iași. She gave it to Chiyo. Nobody needed to translate.

After dessert, someone suggested going up to Isabelle’s, to Odile’s piano. They all went, in single file up the stairs, Viorica supported by Petrescu, Chiyo carried on a chair by Farid and Julien, like a queen. Chiyo sat down at the piano. Her fingers were stiff and twisted with age, but as soon as they touched the keys, they found forty years of habit again. She played Henri’s waltz, which Haruka had sent her as a recording the year before and which she had learnt by ear. Viorica sat down beside her on the bench. At the silence, Chiyo lifted her hands. Viorica played her three notes, with one finger. Chiyo played the next three. Then they finished the waltz together, four hands.

That evening, Amina counted seven languages in Odile’s flat: French, Romanian, Japanese, Farid’s Dari, Monsieur Haddad’s Arabic, the Breton of Nathalie, who only knew swear words but knew all of them, and the English of Aoi, who was the only one who could talk to everyone. She noted it in her spreadsheet. Then, before leaving, Chiyo gave Isabelle her present. It was a small black cast-iron bell, with a paper tongue hanging at the end of a string: a fūrin, a wind chime. Haruka explained that in Japan they are hung at windows in summer, so that the wind becomes music. Chiyo wanted it hung in Odile’s lime tree.

Haruka translated what her grandmother had added. “She says the wind is someone passing by. You can’t see it, but thanks to the bell, you know it has come. She says Madame Odile must be a little like the wind now.” Isabelle took the bell in her hands. She couldn’t answer right away. She bowed to Chiyo, clumsily, Western-style, too low and too long. Chiyo smiled and took her hand. Simone Roux, from the sofa, declared that she wanted the same bell for her balcony in Villeurbanne, so that Philippe would know, when he phoned, that she wasn’t alone: there would at least be the wind.

That night Rose-Hélène hardly slept. She had taken Odile’s letter out of her drawer and put it on her pillow. She knew the envelope by heart: the slightly yellowed paper, the slanting, hurried handwriting, the four words “For Rose-Hélène. For later.”, and a little drawing in the corner, a lime blossom, which Odile had done in pencil and which faded a little more each year. For seven years she had waited to find out when “later” would be. She had asked everyone. Nobody had been able to answer. Around four in the morning she fell asleep, the letter against her cheek, knowing one thing: tomorrow, she would find out.

On Monday 3 May, the sky was grey. The forecast said rain for late morning. Isabelle looked at the sky from the window at six, then at a quarter past six, then at half past six, as if her gaze could change something. Simone Roux phoned her at seven to tell her it wouldn’t rain. Isabelle asked her how she knew. Simone replied that she had warned the sky the evening before, from her balcony, and that at ninety-two you know how to talk to the sky. At nine, the clouds parted above Fourvière hill. By ten, the sun was blazing.

The La Duchère garden filled up slowly, then very quickly. There were the people of the district, of course, the neighbours from the tower blocks, the schoolchildren with their teachers. There was the whole Thursday orchestra, with its folding music stands. And there were, from all over France, forty-three musicians, one for each orchestra in the network, each with an instrument and a small sign bearing the name of their town. A bagpiper from Brest, in a kilt. A fisherman from Marseille, Monsieur Benhamou’s cousin, who had brought the flag of the boat “Belle-Mère”. Three teenagers from Clermont-Ferrand who had been among the sixty-three children of the letter to the mayor and who were now sixteen.

There were also faces nobody expected. Arnaud Desforges, the former Minister of Culture, who hadn’t been a minister for four years, had come by train, like an ordinary citizen, with his daughter Clémence, eighteen, her violin on her back, who was now studying at the Paris Conservatoire. Madame Lefort, the examiner with the red scarf, was there with Monsieur Abadie, who had put on a tie. Madame Chevalier, Rose-Hélène’s former teacher, now retired, had come with her whole former class, now in their last year of primary school. Monsieur Rollet and Léa were there, and, right at the back, half hidden behind a tree, Valère Dumontel, who had taken the six o’clock TGV without telling anyone.

Gérard had closed his café for the day, something that hadn’t happened since his mother’s funeral in 2019. He had hung a piece of cardboard on the door on which he had written in felt-tip: “Closed on account of garden”. The op-ed club had come as a block, in suits, with the morning paper under their arms, out of habit. Thiébaut, the luthier, eighty-five, was sitting on a folding chair in the front row next to Simone, explaining to anyone who would listen that the lime tree in the garden, once cut down, would make an excellent violin, which shocked the children very much. Nathalie had come with Loïc, who had never seen so many trees and so many people without a drop of salt water around.

Chiyo’s fūrin had been hung in the lime tree at dawn by Farid, standing on Bernard Delorme’s stepladder, under the direction of Chiyo, who had spent twenty minutes choosing the branch. It now hung above the plaque covered by its white sheet, and every time a little wind passed through, it made a small clear sound, like a drop of water on glass. The children of the district came to look at it up close. A little girl asked Rose-Hélène if it was for calling someone. Rose-Hélène thought about it and said no, it was rather for answering. The little girl nodded, as if it were obvious.

At ten, Rose-Hélène arrived with Julien and Isabelle, an hour before everyone else, as planned. She had Odile’s letter in her jacket pocket. They talked for a while by the plaque. She said she would open the letter at the moment the sheet was taken off, not before. Isabelle said her mother would have liked that. Then Viorica and Chiyo got off the bus together, arm in arm, one’s stick in the other’s hand, each talking in her own language and laughing at things nobody else could understand. Rose-Hélène watched them cross the park. She thought that perhaps this was the answer to all her questions.

It was then that she noticed him for the first time. Behind the wall of the Jeanne-Valmont media library, half hidden by a bush, there was a boy. He must have been eight. He was wearing a red anorak far too big for him, with sleeves that covered his hands, and he was watching the crowd with big serious eyes, not daring to come closer. He wasn’t with anyone. When Rose-Hélène caught his eye, he hid behind the bush. She wanted to go over to him, but at that moment Henri-Ion tugged at her sleeve because the mayor was arriving, and when she turned round, the boy had gone.

The Thursday committee had turned itself into a team of stewards for the occasion. Inès, with a badge and a walkie-talkie borrowed from the city hall, directed operations the way a lawyer runs a trial. Amina counted people at the entrance with a mechanical clicker she had bought specially, and announced the figures every ten minutes: six hundred, seven hundred and fifty, nine hundred, one thousand and two. Bertrand handed out the programmes, which he had written himself and which began with “Provisional schedule of the ceremony”. Sami and Farid carried chairs for the elderly. Philippe Roux, up from Paris for the second time in three days, helped them, in his suit, with an engineer’s efficiency that impressed everyone.

At eleven o’clock sharp, the mayor of Lyon spoke at a microphone set up next to the lime tree. He was a man of about sixty, used to official speeches. He began in the purest administrative style. He spoke of “the naming of this emblematic site”, “the recognition of civic engagement” and “the promotion of our city’s intangible heritage”. There were many nominalisations and not many living people in his sentences. Monsieur Castaing nodded knowingly. The schoolchildren were starting to fidget. After three minutes, nobody was really listening any more, except Bertrand, who was taking notes.

Then the mayor did something nobody expected. He folded up the sheet with his speech, put it in his pocket and said, in a different voice: “I’m going to tell you the truth. My grandmother lived in the Croix-Rousse. She was one of Doctor Bernard’s patients. When I was ten, I used to fetch her medicines from the chemist’s, and Doctor Bernard always gave me a mint sweet, telling me not to tell my grandmother. I never told. I’m telling it today, in front of a thousand people, because I think she would forgive me.” There was a silence, then laughter, then applause that the administration hadn’t planned.

Bernard Delorme spoke next, as city councillor and rapporteur for the project. He was brief, which was new for him. He recalled that in 2028, on the city council, he had voted against the creation of the first Thursday orchestra, because he thought it was money thrown out of the window. He said he had been wrong, that it was the biggest mistake of his political career and the best one of his life, since it had allowed him to play the trumpet every Thursday and to sound a foghorn in front of a minister. Monique, in the front row, rolled her eyes, but she was smiling.

Then it was Isabelle’s turn. She had no notes. She stood at the microphone, looked at the crowd, the lime tree, the covered plaque, and spoke simply, the way her mother used to speak. She told of Odile’s arrival in Lyon, fifty-two years earlier, and the first sentence of her first notebook. She said she hadn’t written the book: her mother had, her father had, and everyone who was there. She said the silence Odile had left had filled with voices. And she ended by asking everyone, when they went home that evening, to leave their door ajar, just enough for someone to be able to knock. Then she fell silent, and the fūrin chimed in the lime tree.

All that remained was to take off the sheet. Isabelle had decided it would be neither the mayor nor herself, but the oldest and the youngest people present. The oldest was Viorica, ninety-seven. The youngest was Awa, who was two and didn’t quite understand what she was being asked to do, but thought the idea of pulling on a sheet was excellent. Viorica went up to the plaque, leaning on Petrescu. Amina put Awa down on the ground. Each of them took a corner of the sheet. Viorica counted to three, in Romanian. Awa pulled on “two”, which made everyone laugh, and the white sheet fell onto the grass.

The plaque was of pale stone, with letters engraved and painted blue, the same blue as the door on the cover. “Jardin Odile-Bernard (1950-2031). Doctor, neighbour, musician of silence. Leave your door open.” The crowd applauded for a long time. Photographers took pictures. The mayor shook hands. And while everyone was looking at the plaque, Rose-Hélène stepped a few paces away, under the branches of the lime tree, where there was a little shade. Haruka, who had been keeping an eye on her, came over without a word and handed her Odile’s pencil to open the envelope. Rose-Hélène slid it under the flap and opened it very gently, so as not to damage the lime blossom drawn in the corner.

There was a single sheet, folded in two, covered in Odile’s small hurried handwriting, the handwriting of her notebooks. Rose-Hélène read. “My little Rose-Hélène, if you are reading this letter, it means you can read. Well done. You asked me one day why there was a silence in the middle of the waltz. I told you it was for breathing. That was true, but it wasn’t everything. Silence is the space you leave for someone else. If you play everything, all the time, nobody can get into the music.”

“Later isn’t a date. It’s the day when you won’t need me any more to know what to do. If you have opened this letter, it means that day has come, and I have nothing left to teach you. I only want to ask you one thing. Look around you. There is surely someone, not far away, who has just arrived and doesn’t know anyone. Someone whistling three notes in their corner, hoping that someone will answer. Go to them. Give them my key. Not so that they can open my door: it has never been closed. So that they know someone is waiting for them.”

“And don’t forget to eat something before you cry. Emotions are facts too, but they’re easier to bear on a full stomach. Lots of love, my little neighbour. Answer. Odile.” At the bottom of the sheet there were three small musical notes drawn in pencil, a little shaky. Rose-Hélène read the letter twice. She didn’t cry. She put her hand in her pocket, where there was a biscuit Ioana had given her that morning, and ate it, very seriously, in two bites, under Haruka’s astonished gaze. Then she said: “I understand. It was today.”

She looked around her. There were a thousand people in the garden. How could she find among them someone who had just arrived and didn’t know anyone? She thought of Chiyo, but Chiyo had Haruka, and now Viorica. She thought of Loïc, but Loïc had Nathalie. She thought of Valère Dumontel, hidden behind his tree, but he at least knew Isabelle, even if he would have preferred otherwise. Everyone here had someone. That was exactly the problem: in a garden full of people who knew each other, the one who knew nobody must be somewhere on the edge, where nobody was looking.

That was when she heard it. Not loud. Almost nothing. Three whistled notes, hesitant, a little out of tune, coming from behind the wall of the media library. The first three notes of the waltz. Rose-Hélène froze. She knew that whistle. She had heard it three days earlier, on the evening of 30 April, when she was sitting on the bench with Isabelle and someone, behind a lit window on the eighth floor of the big tower block, had answered her three notes. She had thought it was chance. It wasn’t chance. She gave the pencil back to Haruka, slipped the letter into her pocket and crossed the crowd.

The boy in the red anorak was sitting on the ground, his back against the wall, his knees under his chin. When he saw Rose-Hélène coming, he jumped up to run away. So she stopped, a few metres from him, and whistled the next three notes of the waltz. The boy stopped too. He turned round. He looked at her suspiciously, then curiously. He whistled three notes. She whistled the three after that. They went on like that, three notes each, to the end of the waltz’s first phrase, without saying a word, among the bushes, while twenty metres away a thousand people were applauding a plaque.

His name was Yassin. He was eight. He had arrived from Sudan in January with his mother and his little sister Amal, after a journey he didn’t want to talk about. They lived on the eighth floor of the big tower block on the other side of the park. He went to the local school, in a special class for children learning French, and he already spoke a little, in short, careful sentences. He didn’t have any friends yet. Rose-Hélène asked him how he knew the waltz. He pointed at the media library. On Thursday evenings, he explained, he opened his window and heard the music coming out of the hall. He had learnt the notes by himself.

Rose-Hélène untied the blue ribbon she wore round her neck. There were three keys on it. She took the oldest one, the key to Odile’s flat on rue d’Austerlitz, with its little cardboard label on which Odile had written “Door” in pencil. She held it out to Yassin. He looked at it without taking it. He asked, in his careful French: “It is the key to what?” Rose-Hélène said: “To a door that’s always open.” Yassin frowned, like someone doing a difficult sum. “Then why a key?” Rose-Hélène smiled. She had the answer in her pocket, written in pencil. “So that you know someone is waiting for you.”

Yassin took the key. He held it tightly in his closed hand, the way Farid held his stone. Rose-Hélène led him towards the lime tree, through the crowd. Isabelle saw them coming. She saw the key in the boy’s hand and the blue ribbon with only two keys round Rose-Hélène’s neck, and she understood without needing an explanation. She crouched down in front of Yassin, at his height. She said to him slowly, articulating every word: “Rue d’Austerlitz, number twelve, third floor. On Thursdays, after the music, there’s soup. Come whenever you like. You don’t need to knock.” Yassin nodded. He had understood the essential, as Monsieur Delattre would have said.

At that moment a young woman in a green headscarf came running up, with a little girl in her arms, looking frightened. It was Yassin’s mother, who had been looking for him for half an hour. She spoke almost no French. She saw her son with a key in his hand, among strangers, and she was afraid. Monsieur Haddad stepped forward and spoke to her gently in Arabic. He explained who these people were, what this garden was and what the key meant. The young woman listened. Then she put her hand on her heart and said a word that everyone understood, because it existed, almost the same, in many languages: “Thank you.”

While the adults were talking, Yassin’s little sister Amal, who was four, had wriggled out of her mother’s arms. She had found Awa, who was two, at the foot of the lime tree. The two little girls had no language in common, neither Arabic nor French nor anything at all, since Awa could still only say about twenty words. They looked at each other very seriously. Then Awa held out to Amal the little red plastic harmonica Rose-Hélène had given her when she was born, which she never let go of. Amal blew into it. It made a dreadful noise. The two little girls burst out laughing. Amina, watching the scene, told Bertrand that, statistically, it was the beginning of a friendship.

It was noon. Julien stepped up onto the little platform set up next to the lime tree. Behind him, the Thursday orchestra and the forty-three musicians from all over France had gathered, with their instruments, their signs and their folding stands: violins, flutes, bagpipes, trumpets, an oud, a triangle, a double bass, Haruka’s violin, Clémence’s, Farid’s rubab, Bernard Delorme’s trumpet and, at his feet, the foghorn. Simone Roux had taken out Lucien’s clarinet. Chiyo was sitting in the front row with Viorica. Julien raised his arms. A thousand people fell silent. And the orchestra began Henri’s waltz.

It was the first time the waltz had been played in the garden that bore Odile’s name. It sounded different in the open air, between the tower blocks, under the blue sky. The violins rose towards the windows, and at the windows of the towers people appeared, one by one, to listen. The Brest bagpipes gave the theme something of the sea. Farid’s rubab added a colour the waltz had never had, from very far away, from a valley where music had been silenced for years. Rose-Hélène was playing Henri’s harmonica, next to Yassin, who was still holding his key. And then the waltz reached the seventeenth bar, and the orchestra stopped.

Silence fell over the garden. The silence of a thousand people, which is the most impressive silence there is. Nobody coughed. The children stopped moving. Even the pigeons on the roof of the media library seemed to be waiting. One bar. Two. On the third, a breath of wind passed through the lime tree, and Chiyo’s fūrin chimed, just once, very clearly. Chiyo closed her eyes. Four. On the fifth bar, Bernard Delorme sounded the foghorn, long and low, like a ship coming into port. Six. Seven. And on the eighth bar, before anyone else could do it, a small voice whistled three notes, all alone, a little out of tune, but in their place.

It was Yassin. He had whistled without thinking, because that was what he did every Thursday evening at his eighth-floor window, when the music stopped and nobody answered. This time, someone answered. Rose-Hélène whistled the next three notes. Then Simone played the three after, on the clarinet. Then Chiyo hummed them, Viorica whistled them, Haruka played them on the violin, and little by little, from person to person, the whole garden began to whistle, a thousand people, children, old people, a former minister, a Paris publisher hidden behind a tree and, at the windows of the towers, people nobody knew. Then the orchestra took up the waltz again and played it to the end.

After the waltz, the garden took a long time to empty. Nobody wanted to be the first to leave. The forty-three musicians from all over France mingled with the Thursday orchestra and went on playing anything at all, tunes from their regions, a Breton jig, a Marseille song, a bourrée from the Auvergne that the Clermont-Ferrand teenagers danced to, laughing. Clémence Desforges asked Haruka if she could play next to her. The Marseille fisherman planted the flag of the “Belle-Mère” at the foot of the lime tree, next to the plaque, saying that this way Yves and Henri would know where to find Odile. Nobody dared tell him it wasn’t allowed. Not even the mayor.

In the afternoon, in the Huit Mesures hall of the media library, Isabelle signed books for four hours. The queue stretched out of the hall, across the lobby and down into the park. Isabelle didn’t know how to sign a book she hadn’t written. She ended up finding a formula, which she repeated a thousand times: “For you, from Odile and Henri, through their daughter.” Valère Dumontel queued for fifty minutes, like everyone else, and paid twenty euros for his copy, in cash. Isabelle signed it for him with the same formula, adding only, underneath: “Not a comma.”

Around five, Monsieur Castaing arrived at the signing table, very agitated, the book open in his hand. He had found a mistake. Just one, on page two hundred and fourteen, in the glossary: a grave accent instead of an acute. He was both horrified and delighted. The committee, which had reread every page at least three times, was dismayed. Haruka, who had typed the glossary, turned bright red. Isabelle looked at the mistake for a long time. Then she declared that it would not be corrected, neither in this edition nor in the paperback. She said a perfect book would have displeased her mother, and that a chipped cup is mended with gold. Chiyo, when it was translated for her, applauded three times.

In the evening, when everyone had come back to rue d’Austerlitz, exhausted, Rose-Hélène sat down next to Isabelle on Odile’s sofa. She said it was now 3 May and she had the right to read the last page. Isabelle opened the book at the end. After Haruka’s glossary, after page two hundred and fourteen and its crooked accent, there was one last page. It reproduced, in facsimile, the last page of Odile’s last notebook, written in August 2031, a few days before her death. There was just one word, in the middle of the blank page, in her slanting handwriting, grown shaky: “Answer.” And underneath, nothing more.

“Is that all?” asked Rose-Hélène. Isabelle said yes, that was all. Rose-Hélène looked for a long time at the blank page below the word. Then she said she understood. The blank page was like the eight bars. It was the space you left. Isabelle said: “The rest is for us to write.” In the kitchen, Viorica and Chiyo were drinking herbal tea, each talking in her own language. Farid was tuning his rubab. Simone was asleep in the armchair, Lucien’s clarinet on her knees. And on the other side of the city, on the eighth floor of a tower block in La Duchère, an eight-year-old boy was falling asleep with a key in his hand.

On 4 May, Viorica left for Bucharest. On the platform at Part-Dieu there were almost as many people as when she arrived, with less lily of the valley and more tears. She kissed everyone, one by one, starting with Henri-Ion and ending with Simone. She said she would come back the following year. Everyone knew she was ninety-seven, and she knew it too, but nobody said anything, because it was a promise, and you don’t correct a promise. As the train pulled away, she lowered the window, against the rules, and whistled three notes. On the platform, about a hundred people answered. The ticket inspector pretended not to hear anything.

Ten years later, on 4 March 2048, Rose-Hélène turned twenty. She was a student at the École des beaux-arts in Lyon, in the illustration department, and she had already drawn the covers of six books, including the Japanese translation of “Leave your door open”, done by Haruka and published in Kyoto. The book had been translated into eleven languages. The Éditions Saint-Clair paperback was in its fourteenth reprint, without a comma changed, with its crooked accent on page two hundred and fourteen, which readers all over the world pointed out every year in letters to the publisher, and to whom Valère Dumontel replied every year, personally, that it was intentional.

Many things had changed in ten years. Haruka was first violin with the Orchestre national de Lyon, and she still spent her Thursday evenings with the neighbourhood orchestra. Farid had been an A&E nurse at the Édouard-Herriot hospital for seven years, and he played the rubab in a small band that got Afghan weddings dancing all over the region. The network had sixty-one orchestras. Inès was a lawyer and defended young foreigners in court. Some people had left too, gently, the way you leave after a long journey. Viorica had fallen asleep one evening in 2041, aged exactly one hundred, her diary open on the bedside table. The last line said: “I answered.”

Simone Roux had lived to ninety-nine, at home, in her flat in Gratte-Ciel, as she had wished, with Farid in the back room and Philippe every Sunday, except when the drawing of lots made him the cook, which happened strangely rarely. Chiyo Mori, ninety-four, still sent a postcard from Kyoto every spring, with five lines in French. Isabelle, seventy-eight, still chaired the Thursday committee, which now proofread other people’s books. And Yassin was eighteen. He had just passed his baccalauréat. He played the violin in the Thursday orchestra. And he still had the key.

One Thursday evening that winter, after rehearsal, Rose-Hélène had asked him, half joking, whether he planned to keep it all his life. Yassin had thought about it, with the same frown as when he was eight and doing difficult sums. Then he had said no. One day he would give it to someone. To someone who had just arrived, who didn’t know anyone and who whistled three notes in their corner. Rose-Hélène had asked him when. Yassin had smiled. He had taken the key out of his pocket, with its little cardboard label on which the word “Door” had almost faded away, and had answered: “Not yet. Later.”

On the evening of her birthday, Julien gave Rose-Hélène a large yellowed envelope tied with a ribbon. Hélène had entrusted it to him in 2028, a year before she died, with an instruction: “For Rose-Hélène, for her twentieth birthday.” It was exactly what Henri had written in 1962 on the envelope of a waltz: “For Hélène, for her twentieth birthday.” Rose-Hélène opened the envelope. Inside was the original score of the waltz, the one that Henri, a twenty-two-year-old music student, had written in pencil for Hélène before leaving for Algeria and the sea. The paper was fragile, stained, folded and unfolded a thousand times. Rose-Hélène laid it on the table, very gently.

She followed the staves with her finger, bar by bar, humming. She knew every note. Then she reached the seventeenth bar, the one where all the Thursday orchestras stopped for eight bars of silence. In the original 1962 score there was no silence. There were notes, as everywhere else. But in the margin, right beside it, Henri had written a few words in pencil, so small and so faint that you could hardly see them, and that perhaps nobody had ever noticed. Rose-Hélène had to take a magnifying glass to read them. It said: “Here, one day, leave room.”

Rose-Hélène stayed in front of the score for a long time. Henri had known from the beginning, at twenty-two, without knowing who would come. Odile had done it, decades later, without ever having read those words. And between the two there had been a whole life, thousands of kilometres of sea, a war, a lime tree, an old lady in a care home, a little girl with a harmonica, and thousands of people who had learnt to be silent at the right moment. The next morning, Rose-Hélène took the score to the Jeanne-Valmont media library, so that it could be displayed in the Huit Mesures hall, next to Jeanne’s glasses. She kept only a photo of the margin.

That day, as she left the media library, she crossed the Jardin Odile-Bernard. The lime tree had grown a lot. Its branches now reached beyond the plaque and covered the bench in light shade. Chiyo’s fūrin was still hanging there, a little rusty, and it chimed when the wind passed. Children were playing on the lawn. Old people were reading on the benches. Rose-Hélène sat down where Odile used to sit to talk to the trees, where she herself had sat ten years earlier with Isabelle, a bottle of water in her hand. She closed her eyes. Then, without thinking, she whistled the first three notes of the waltz.

Somewhere in the garden, a small voice whistled the next three. A child’s voice, a little hesitant, a little out of tune, but in its place. Rose-Hélène opened her eyes. There were about twenty children on the lawn, running, shouting, hiding behind the trees, and she didn’t know which one had whistled. She didn’t try to find out. She didn’t need to. She knew that somewhere, someone had just arrived, didn’t know anyone yet, and had learnt three notes by listening at an open window. In the lime tree, the fūrin chimed. Rose-Hélène smiled. She answered.

Reading text: Isabelle’s speech

At the inauguration of the garden, after the mayor’s official speech, Isabelle spoke simply, without notes. Here is what she said. Notice the time expressions and the emphasis. Listen to the text twice, then read it aloud. At the end, answer 4 questions. This is the last text of level B2.
Discours d’Isabelle au jardin
Fifty-two years ago, my mother arrived in Lyon. She didn’t know anyone. In her first notebook she wrote: “Good: I’ll be able to listen.” From that day on, she never stopped.

For forty-five years she listened to her patients, her neighbours, her trees. She listened to a little girl who knocked at her door with a harmonica. She listened to a silence of eight bars, and she heard in it something nobody had heard before her.
I’m not the one who wrote this book. She did, my father did, and all of you did. All I did was turn the pages, for eight months, with a committee that never left me in peace.

It’s been seven years since she left. I thought the silence she had left behind would never be filled. I was wrong. It filled with voices, with music, with people I didn’t know and whom I will never leave.
In a moment we are going to take the sheet off this plaque. On it you will read three words she often repeated. They are neither orders nor advice. They are an invitation.
So when you go home tonight, do one single thing for her. Don’t close your door completely. Leave it ajar, just enough for someone to be able to knock. And when they knock, answer.

The last assignment of level B2. Write (at least 300 words) a letter “for later”, addressed to yourself ten years from now: what you have learnt, who helped you, what you hope for. Use as many B2 structures as you can.
I used “il y a”, “depuis” and “pendant” correctly.
I used at least one subjunctive after a time conjunction (avant que, jusqu’à ce que).
I emphasised an idea with “c’est… qui” or “c’est… que”.
I made a past participle agree correctly with a direct object placed before it.
I used at least one complex negation (ne… que, ni… ni, ne… plus personne).
I used a past conditional for a regret and a future perfect for a plan.
Two years ago I couldn’t say hello in French. Since then I have studied almost every day.
It’s by reading stories that I learnt the most.
The sentences I wrote at the beginning make me smile today.
If I had started earlier, I might have been less patient. I regret nothing.
When you read this letter, you will probably have reached level C1. Keep going until the language is yours.
